newsitem.title: USA: Dow racks up 40th record close so far this year.
newsitem.headline: Dow racks up 40th record close so far this year.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average Tuesday raced to its 40th record close this year, propelled by another drop in long-term interest rates and a rally in the stock of International Business Machines Corp.
The blue-chip Dow ended up 50.69 points at 6,397.60, setting its ninth record out of the past 10 trading sessions, and beating Friday's high of 6,348.03.
It slipped 1 point Monday after rallying more than 350 points in the previous two weeks.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,435 to 1,008 on active volume of 454 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"What a great tape. Oh my God! It's the most powerful bull market of all time and has the horses to go higher," said James Cramer of Cramer Co.
"The true leadership is Microsoft, Intel and IBM," he said. "It feels like '85 and '86. The market wants to go somewhere and it has to travel a lot of points to get there."

The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 5.14 to 742.16, topping the old record close of 737.62 set Friday. The NYSE Composite gained 1.90 to 391.80, also topping Friday's record 390.02.
IBM rallied 6-3/4 to 153-3/4, climbing nearly 20 points since Thursday as Wall Street analysts raised their price targets for the giant computer maker's stock.
Other high-technology stocks were also big gainers, with Microsoft Corp. surging 5-1/2 to 155-7/8 and Intel up 5-3/8 to 120-3/4.
In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond rose 14/32, sending its yield down to 6.44 percent from 6.47 percent at Monday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Bonds rose after October housing starts fell 5.1 percent to an annualized 1.366 million rate, the lowest since October 1995.
The data provided further proof that the economy is slowing and there is no reason to worry that the Federal Reserve will need to raise interest rates to slow growth.
"The bond's going to six percent, so you're not making money there," Cramer said.
"The consumer domestic economy is slowing down. But the corporate domestic economy is fine and and the international corporate economy is also doing well," he said.
But Ralph Bloch, chief technical analyst at Raymond James, remains cautious. "IBM is like the market. It's standing on a stilt. We're in an acceleration phase, a straight up move."
He said that mutual fund managers were uneasy about buying stocks at current levels.

"There's no doubt in my mind that the buying going on here by managers is very nervous and they're buying even though they wish they didn't have to," he said. "They, too, don't know how long the ball will stay in the air. They'd never get fired for having IBM or Intel or Microsoft and stuff like that in their portfolios."
Among individual stocks, Kmart rose 1-1/2 to 11-1/8 on speculation that it was in takeover talks with Kohlberg Kravis & Roberts. Both companies declined to comment.
Hewlett-Packard rose 2-5/8 to 52-3/4. Analysts said they expected the computer maker to post stronger results, just one day after it reported disapppointing profits for its fiscal fourth quarter.
Compaq rose 4 to 80-3/8. A senior company executive forecast a strong first half 1997 for Compaq at the Comdex computer trade show in Las Vegas.
Rainforest Cafe lost 2-1/4 to 28-1/4 on news that its president and chief operating officer had taken a 30-day leave of absence for personal reasons.
Citicorp rose 1-3/4 to 106-7/8 after expanding its stock buyback by $4 billion to $8.5 billion.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 8.05 points to 1,262.62. The American Stock Exchange index edged up 0.46 to 584.64.
The average NYSE share was up 20 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at a new high of 7,153.891 up 35.405 or 0.50 percent.
